introduction: The protocol aims to investigate how intervention and individual characteristics moderate the effects of chronic exercise on overall depression severity and on depression symptoms in older adults. The authors hypothesize that the effects differ across these characteristics.
methodology: The paper is a protocol for a systematic and meta-analytic review of randomized controlled trials in older adults with a mean age of at least 60 years. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction and quality assessment, and a third reviewer resolves disagreements. Searches include Web of Science, CINAHL and APA Psycinfo. Analysis uses random-effects models with Hedges' g in Comprehensive Meta-Analysis 4.0 and R.
theory: The protocol says it is guided by PRISMA-P; no theory is named.
results: The paper is a protocol and reports no results.
discussion: The authors expect a moderate effect of exercise on depression compared to active and passive control groups. They expect the results to be moderated by intervention and individual characteristics. They say their review will be the first to examine effects on different symptoms of depression in older adults.
limitations: The authors say excluding RCTs with pharmacological or psychotherapy effects means no conclusions can be drawn for add-on exercise. They anticipate heterogeneous data and wide variance in how exercise and individual characteristics are reported. They suggest the review may reveal research gaps for further RCTs.

introduction.q: this protocol outlines a review aiming to investigate how the above-mentioned intervention characteristics and individual characteristics moderate the effects of chronic exercise on overall depression severity and the different symptoms of depression in older adults

We hypothesize that chronic exercise interventions differ in their efficacy in reducing overall depression severity and the different symptoms of depression in older adults across participants with different individual’s characteristics

methodology.q: This protocol is guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P).
older adults with a mean age of at least 60 years
We will use the Population-Intervention-Comparator-Outcome-Study design (PICOS) criteria to determine primary study inclusion.
Two independent reviewers will conduct the study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment.
Disagreement will be solved by a third reviewer.
The following electronic databases will be searched from inception to shortly before publishing the meta-analysis: Web of Science (all bases); Academic Search Complete
methodology.loc: Method, Information sources and search strategy

methodology.q: Summary effects will be calculated as Hedges’ g using random-effects weights.
All analyses will be performed using the software Comprehensive Meta-Analysis 4.0 and R.

theory.q: This protocol is guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P).

results.q: In this article, we have outlined a protocol for a systematic and meta-analytic review

discussion.q: we expect to find a moderate effect of exercise on depression compared to active and passive control groups
We further expect the results to be moderated by intervention characteristics and individual characteristics
Our meta-analytical review will be the first that examines the effects of chronic exercise on different symptoms of depression in older adults

limitations.q: Besides the above-mentioned strengths, the study has some limitations as well.
We plan to exclude RCTs with tested effects of pharmacological treatment and / or psychotherapy. Therefore, no conclusions can be drawn for exercise interventions as add-on treatment.
We further anticipate limitations in form of heterogenous data and a wide variance in the reporting of the exercise characteristics (e.g., detailedness) and the individual characteristics.
the review results may reveal research gaps that can stimulate the formulation of research questions for further RCTs

abstract_claims.q: There is high evidence that chronic exercise benefits overall depression severity in older adults.
The results of the proposed review are anticipated to have a substantial impact on research and clinical practice.
On the one hand, the review’s conclusions could form the foundation for developing evidence-based recommendations for individualized exercise programs that alleviate depression in older adults.
On the other hand, by revealing research gaps, the review results could encourage the formulation of research questions for further RCTs.
